```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

## The model

LEWIS (Laplace Error Working model for Inference and Selection of DAG)
learns a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from data in which each variable is
a linear function of its parents plus an independent error. Some errors
may be Gaussian and others non-Gaussian. LEWIS uses a Laplace error working
model and a complexity prior on the DAG. It samples DAGs from an
approximate posterior and then estimates the distribution equivalence
class of the DAG. This class is represented by a restricted partially
directed acyclic graph (RPDAG). An edge of the RPDAG is directed when the
data determine its direction, and undirected otherwise.

The method is described in Chaudhuri, Bhattacharya, Sarkar and Ni (2026),
"Consistent DAG Selection for Bayesian Causal Discovery under Model
Misspecification", manuscript.

## A simulated example

We simulate 500 observations of 6 variables from the DAG
x1 -> x2, x1 -> x3, x2 -> x4, x3 -> x4, x4 -> x5, x5 -> x6.
The errors of x1, x4 and x5 are Laplace. The errors of x2, x3 and x6 are
Gaussian.

```{r data}
library(LEWIS)

set.seed(2025)
n <- 500
laplace <- function(n) (rexp(n) - rexp(n)) / sqrt(2)
x1 <- laplace(n)
x2 <- 0.8 * x1 + rnorm(n)
x3 <- -0.7 * x1 + rnorm(n)
x4 <- 0.6 * x2 + 0.6 * x3 + laplace(n)
x5 <- 0.8 * x4 + laplace(n)
x6 <- 0.7 * x5 + rnorm(n)
X <- cbind(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)
```

The true RPDAG follows from the true DAG and the set of nodes with
non-Gaussian errors.

```{r truth}
true_dag <- matrix(0, 6, 6, dimnames = list(colnames(X), colnames(X)))
true_dag["x1", "x2"] <- 1
true_dag["x1", "x3"] <- 1
true_dag["x2", "x4"] <- 1
true_dag["x3", "x4"] <- 1
true_dag["x4", "x5"] <- 1
true_dag["x5", "x6"] <- 1
true_rpdag <- rpdag(true_dag, nG = c("x1", "x4", "x5"))
true_rpdag
```

## Fitting LEWIS

The default settings are those of the paper: the complexity prior with
`d = 0.03` and `alpha = 0.75`, a start at the estimate of the TL method,
10,000 iterations for up to 20 variables, a burn-in of 20 percent, at most
8000 kept draws, the Shapiro-Wilk level 0.05 / p and the 95 percent
credible ball.

```{r fit}
fit <- lewis(X, seed = 1)
fit
```

The point estimate `D_hat` is an RPDAG. `D_hat[i, j] = 1` and
`D_hat[j, i] = 0` means the edge i -> j. A pair with both entries equal to 1
is an undirected edge. A pair with both entries equal to 0 has no edge.

```{r dhat}
fit$D_hat
shd(fit$D_hat, true_rpdag)
```

## The edges and the nodes

For each edge of the point estimate, `prob` is the posterior probability
that the edge has the same status as in `D_hat`, and `prob_adjacent` is the
posterior probability that the two nodes are adjacent.

```{r edges}
fit$edges
```

For each node, `prob_nongaussian` is the proportion of draws in which its
error is declared non-Gaussian.

```{r nodes}
fit$nodes
```

## The shape of the posterior and the credible ball

The table `graphs` lists the distinct RPDAGs of the kept draws, in
decreasing order of posterior mass. Each graph is compared with `D_hat`.
Its class is identical, upper (every edge of `D_hat` is in the graph with
the same status), lower (every edge of the graph is in `D_hat` with the
same status) or rearranged (otherwise).

```{r graphs}
head(fit$graphs[, c("rank", "mass", "class", "shd", "added", "removed", "reversed")])
```

The 95 percent credible ball holds every graph within SHD `radius` of
`D_hat`.

```{r ball}
fit$ball
summary(fit)
```

## Plots

```{r plots, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit)                 # the point estimate
plot(fit, type = "ball")  # posterior mass by SHD from the point estimate
plot(fit, type = "edges") # posterior probabilities of the edges
```

## Changing the settings

The uniform prior on DAGs is obtained with `d = 0`.

```{r uniform}
fit_uniform <- lewis(X, d = 0, n_iter = 4000, seed = 1)
fit_uniform$D_hat
```

The chain can start at the empty graph, or at any DAG given as an adjacency
matrix with the parents in the rows.

```{r start}
fit_empty <- lewis(X, start = "empty", n_iter = 4000, seed = 1)
fit_true <- lewis(X, start = true_dag, n_iter = 4000, seed = 1)
shd(fit_empty$D_hat, fit_true$D_hat)
```

The number of iterations is set with `n_iter`. The burn-in fraction and the
largest number of kept draws are set with `burn_in` and `max_draws`.
`max_draws = Inf` keeps every draw after the burn-in. `lewis_schedule()`
shows the schedule for a given number of variables.

```{r schedule}
lewis_schedule(6)
lewis_schedule(50)
lewis_schedule(6, n_iter = 20000, max_draws = Inf)
```

## Checking convergence

The trace of the score should show no trend after the burn-in.

```{r trace}
plot(fit, type = "trace")
fit$diagnostics$ess_log_score
```

LEWIS gives a warning when the effective sample size of the score is below
`ess_min` (100 by default). With `n_chains = 2` or more, further chains
start at the empty graph and at the TL estimate. LEWIS then reports the
potential scale reduction factor of the score and of the number of edges,
and the largest difference between the chains in the posterior
probabilities of adjacencies and orientations. It gives a warning when a
potential scale reduction factor is above 1.05 or a difference is above
0.1.

```{r chains}
fit2 <- lewis(X, n_chains = 2, seed = 1)
fit2$diagnostics[c("psrf_log_score", "psrf_n_edges",
                   "max_diff_adjacency", "max_diff_orientation")]
```

If a warning appears, increase `n_iter` and run the chains again.

## A real-data example

The data set `tcga_prostate` contains the data of the prostate cancer
analysis of the paper: the expression of 8 genes of the androgen-receptor
program in 462 primary prostate tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas. The
genes are the androgen receptor AR, the transcription factors FOXA1 and
HOXB13, and 5 of their target genes. Each gene is adjusted for age, tumor
purity and tissue source site, centered and scaled (see `?tcga_prostate`).

```{r tcga-data}
dim(tcga_prostate)
colnames(tcga_prostate)
```

The data are already centered, so we use `center = FALSE`, as in the
paper. To keep this vignette fast, we run a short chain of 20,000
iterations. This is for illustration only. The paper uses $10^7$
iterations (`n_iter = 1e7`) and checks convergence with several chains,
because shorter chains started from different graphs did not agree on these
data. A short chain may therefore give a warning about the effective
sample size.

```{r tcga-fit}
fit_tcga <- lewis(tcga_prostate, n_iter = 20000, center = FALSE, seed = 1)
fit_tcga
fit_tcga$nodes
```

```{r tcga-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit_tcga)
```

For a real analysis, run the chain of the paper and check convergence:

```{r tcga-long, eval = FALSE}
fit_long <- lewis(tcga_prostate, n_iter = 1e7, center = FALSE, n_chains = 2,
                  seed = 1)
```
